claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu is used as a thin-film protective coating on a conventional metal substrate.
The relevant intervention is wear testing at approximately 800–900 °C rather than at room temperature.
Reciprocating wear under controlled cyclic loading is an applicable test configuration at 800–900 °C.
At 800–900 °C, sufficient thermal energy produces pronounced oxidation of FeNiCrCoCu during wear.
High-temperature wear forms a continuous and adherent oxide film on the FeNiCrCoCu coating surface.
The surface film may be a spinel or a similar mixed-oxide phase.
Elevated-temperature sliding activates tribo-oxidation of the metallic elements in FeNiCrCoCu.
The resulting oxide layer minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact.
The oxide layer changes the wear mode from severe metallic abrasion at room temperature to milder, oxide-governed abrasion at elevated temperature.
At 800–900 °C, FeNiCrCoCu will have lower wear depth than under otherwise comparable room-temperature testing.
At 800–900 °C, FeNiCrCoCu will have a lower coefficient of friction than at room temperature.
Any high-temperature reduction in wear depth and friction is attributable to the protective oxide layer.
At room temperature, the as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has no significant oxide layer.
The room-temperature coating has higher wear and friction because direct metallic abrasion dominates.
The hypothesized protection applies only when the load and temperature induce sufficient tribo-oxidation.
At lower temperatures, oxide formation may be insufficient for the proposed protective mechanism.
At still higher temperatures, excessive oxide spallation may eliminate the protective effect.
The oxide phase identity, adherence, stability, and formation kinetics in FeNiCrCoCu are uncertain.
